data.name: Escape From BioStation
data.detailed_description:
Escape From BioStation is a sci-fi adventure game which places you in the role of a Rob Bot, the last robot citizen of a dangerous ancient space station.You'll take on a host of evil robots armed with your deadly super squirrel.

Tackle a variety of puzzles, platforming challenges and explore the BioStation which is stuffed with loot, hulking bosses, traps… and acorns!

  • Comedy sci-fi adventure story
  • Bizarre and unique puzzles
  • Titanic boss fights
  • Upgrade your squirrel with rapid fire or explosive add-ons
  • Explore the sinister space station from within - and out
  • Immersive Dynamic soundtrack by Alexei Zakharov (X Series) that ups the musical excitement whilst you fight.

data.short_description: Escape From BioStation is an quirky sci-fi comedy adventure game with fast paced combat and unusual puzzles. Take the role of Rob Bot armed with your deadly super squirrel you'll explore and uncover the secret of the BioStation!

reviews.review:
[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Finally, a 3D platformer in which quick reflexes are as importat for shooting as they are for jumping around. Escape From BioStation is Tusky Games’, Steam debut. They wasted no time in setting up the atmosphere since I didn’t get bored at any point while playing this title. You could say that I started reviewing games while focusing and writing about platformers, but they became rather dreary when we’re referring to 2D templates and just certain sprites trying to make a difference from one title to another. The platformer which I review today, didn’t disappoint me especially since it mixes elements from other genres as well.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The dev team made some noticeable efforts in creating humorous situations and dialogue for Escape From BioStation. Right within the first few minutes of starting a new game, you realize that most characters are caricatures of various traits and personalities. We have antagonists in the form of anthropomorphic robots, hovering drones or turrets, yet the true villains are a few humans with delusions of grandeur. Escape From BioStation’s hero, is Rob Bot. A determined protagonist for certain, yet he’s still going to be involved into all sorts of shenanigans which speak much loader than an actual voice could. Most NPCs refer to him simply as Rob and our little robot hero has quite a journey in front of him.

Woken up by a bunch of smugglers which (inefficiently) pose as a rescue team, Rob must traverse the eponymous space station and find a way to let his “rescuers” inside while also point them in the direction of the missile silo. Another devious faction shall emerge halfway through the story and they’re also after these supposedly devastating projectiles aboard the BioStation. Rob plays along and doesn’t reveal his own motivations by preferring that his foes will continue to underestimate him as another “700 year-old rust bucket”. They’re in for a surprise which they won’t be forgetting anytime soon though!

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Escape From BioStation is a pure Unity Engine project. This means, solid performance even on 4K resolution and enough attention to detail to make it stand out from many of its 3D platformer competitors on Steam. While you’ll notice for yourselves that most rooms across the station are dimly lit, I came to the conclusion that this is a deliberate design choice used to highlight the chromatic spectacle in the outdoor levels and the scenery seen from many windows. It’s a step in the right direction since far too many Sci-Fi titles focus on ship or structure interiors without making good use of the spatial backgrounds and potential for visual diversity. 

Staring for hours at metal corridors and neons, both players and the astronauts/droids would consider their surroundings obnoxious soon enough. As I mentioned, I had no problems running the game maxed out and never encountered a single glitch or crash to desktop. Level design is well implemented with aesthetically pleasing assets that are featured even in more narrow sections of the station. The mechanized foes could use a few extra details to separate them from one another. This isn't Clone Wars, right?

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Both the voice acting and the soundtrack are on par with the visuals. Voice synthesizers or not, all characters crack jokes from time to time and the dialogue between them is reason enough to play through Escape From BioStation. You can learn more about the story by accessing the in-game voice logs left by the station captain. Her thick Jamaican accent was always a delight to my ears. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You might say that this title doesn’t take itself too seriously. Why should it? It’s not a “kids’ game” but it doesn’t feature any violence like in the DOOM series either. I consider it a perfect balance between adventure and coherent absurdity. Mark my words though, it is not an easy experience. This is something you’ll come to terms with, from the very first level. It’s no coincidence that Escape From BioStation is featuring the Action and Adventure tags on its Store page. You will shoot at and avoid incoming fire, far more frequently than jumping from one place to another. The more you progress through the storyline, enemies increase both in size and numbers. What are your means of defense? A mechanized squirrel shooting with glowing acorns. You read that correctly. That (synthetic) furry fellow is the most creative weapon I’ve seen since playing the Serious Sam series.

An interesting gameplay mechanic stems from the skillful manner in which you must evade incoming laser bolts/plasma shots/homing missiles while shooting those acorns back at your foes and last but not least, gather your special ammo from the floor as soon as you can. Imagine recovering your arrows after you’ve practiced archery on live targets (I absolutely adore and pick up the bow & arrow in any game that gives me this weapon choice) only that those pesky acorns vanish unless you hurry up. And that means getting dangerously close towards your relenteless enemies. It increases the challenge and you rely on picking up your ammo since you can’t always buy more. I really wish there were more outer space levels, since the lack of gravity always makes “running and gunning” more creative. 

An in-game “vending machine” is present and you can use the coins you collect from previous levels, on all sorts of upgrades to boosh you health pool and increasing the damage output of your ourtlandish weaponry. Sometimes you’ll have to pick up objects, carry them around or avoid obstacles. Your squirrel follows you around and can focus on those puzzle sections. It’s a nice example of variety and break from conventional gameplay at the same time. If you’ll spot more foes, you drop the object you were carrying and pick up your trusty “weapon”. Boss fights require even more planning ahead. They aren’t as cruel as anything Dark Souls might throw at you, but don’t underestimate Escape From BioStation at any point. 

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
I honestly didn’t expect to be so entertained by this title. It just proves that appearances can be so deceiving even after you’ve seen gameplay footage beforehand. Remarkably few flaws as well. Yet Escape From BioStation can get a bit hard at times. Having to restart a level (or section of it) and no option to manually save, did bother me to an extent. Also, the autosave from mid-level gets erased after you exit the game. Make sure that you finished the entire level lest it becomes another issue. At least you can avoid it and the presence of Trading Cards and Achievements shall please all Steam collectors. There, you have no excuse not to discover Rob Bot’s space odyssey by yourselves.

[h1]Strong Points[/h1]
+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Clever use of humor.
+ Perfect mix of action and adventure.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.

[h1]Weak Points[/h1]
- Lack of visual diversity for the enemies.
- Unbalanced difficulty.

[b]Rating 85/100[/b]
